t: Rockefeller and Kipling.
b: An earlier draft of Field Manual IV quoted John D. Rockefeller as saying that the ability to keep your head when all others are losing theirs was a competitive edge. That phrasing is Rudyard Kipling's, from “If—” (1895). I could find no reliable attribution of it to Rockefeller. The point about his temperament stands; the quotation is gone.

t: The Broad Street pump.
b: I had repeated the standard story that John Snow removed the pump handle and stopped the 1854 outbreak. Whitehead's own figures show fatal attacks had already fallen from 142 on 1 September to 14 by the 8th, the day the handle came off, and Snow never claimed otherwise. The entry now says what the evidence says.

t: Harrison's prize.
b: I had written that Harrison was finally paid the longitude prize in 1773. He received £8,750 from Parliament that year and £23,065 in total across all sources — but the statutory £20,000 was never awarded, to him or to anyone.

t: Railway mania mileage.
b: An early draft said roughly 6,000 miles of British railway were authorised at the peak. The 1846 figure is about 9,500 miles across 263 Acts.

t: The EUV consortium.
b: Silicon & Light said an international consortium began work on extreme ultraviolet lithography in 1997. The 1997 consortium, EUV LLC, was American: Intel, AMD and Motorola with three US national laboratories. ASML was admitted in 1999, and that is when the programme became international.

t: Three explanations.
b: The Great Divergence printed '3' as a figure — the explanations still standing. It was my own count, not a sourced number, and the entry itself discusses more than three. It is replaced by Robert Allen's estimate of the return on a spinning jenny: 38% in England against 2.5% in France.

t: Unix and C.
b: The Unix Bargain dated the rewrite of Unix in C to 1972 and called C a language invented so the system could move. Ritchie's own account puts the kernel rewrite in the summer of 1973 and says portability carried little weight at the time; it became the point with the 1977 port to the Interdata 8/32. The entry also said Thompson wrote the first version in three weeks. By his own account it took the month his wife and son were away.

t: A source that did not exist.
b: The Banking Model of Education listed a Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Paulo Freire in its reading list. The Stanford Encyclopedia has no entry on Freire; he appears only inside other articles. The reading list now points to the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry, which does exist. The link had been dead since publication.

t: Six lives said more than their sources.
b: A sourcing pass opened the documents behind the figures in eight lives, and six said more than those documents do. Fritz Haber said roughly half the nitrogen in your body came through his process and that three to four billion people are alive because of it. The first line was found in no document opened. The study most often cited gives 48 per cent of the world's population in 2008, and the entry now says that. John D. Rockefeller put Standard Oil's ninety per cent of American refining in the early 1880s; the source opened puts it at 1879. Andrew Carnegie called the 1901 sale the largest transaction in industrial history; neither source opened says so, and the sentence now says what they do. Robert Moses gave thirteen bridges and hundreds of playgrounds as Caro's count; only the $27 billion was found. Steve Jobs said he paid Lucasfilm for its graphics group; by Alvy Ray Smith's account the new company paid for the technology out of Jobs's ten million. Tu Youyou's sixty laboratories are sixty institutions in the WHO's count. Each figure now carries the document it was read in.

t: Angicos and the printing press.
b: The Banking Model of Education said Freire's workers at Angicos learned to read in forty-five days, and printed 45 days as a figure. The Paulo Freire Institute's own chronology has the lessons running from late January to early April 1963; the programme was named for its forty hours of instruction, after which 300 of the 380 who began were certified literate. The entry now says forty hours. Movable Type said Jeremiah Dittmar's estimate put the growth advantage of early-printing cities at 35 percentage points or more. The paper says over 30, and 35 appears nowhere in it. Both figures had been printed under the promise that they were sourced; neither line named where it came from, and both now do.

t: Borlaug's billion and the Jobs paternity test.
b: Norman Borlaug's entry said estimates of the lives the Green Revolution saved run to a billion or more. The figure is repeated everywhere, and the house found no published calculation behind it; the entry on Tu Youyou already refused the same kind of number. It is gone from Borlaug's entry, and his contested section now says the scale is argued rather than measured. Steve Jobs' entry put the probability of paternity at 94.1 per cent, the figure usually cited to Time in 1983, which the house has not opened. Lisa Brennan-Jobs gives 94.4 per cent in her memoir, and the entry now prints hers, with the source named.

t: Bell Labs' Nobels, and a decade nobody measured.
b: Compounding Machines said ten Nobel Prizes had gone to work done at Bell Labs. The documents opened disagree with each other: one list supports ten prize-years from 1937 to 2023, and the article it sits under says eleven. The entry now says at least ten. The same entry printed '~10 yrs' as a figure for PARC's window of influence. It was the house's own arithmetic on two dates, not a number anyone published, and it has been replaced by the date PARC opened.

t: Who coined microplastics.
b: The Plastic Tide said Richard Thompson coined the word 'microplastics' in 2004, in its opening line, its timeline and its figures. The term appears in marine-pollution work from the 1990s; Thompson's 2004 paper in Science is what put it into circulation. The entry now says that.

t: Three figures in the Press.
b: Movable Type said presses were operating in about 205 European cities by 1500, out of more than a thousand. Neither number is in the paper the entry relies on; Fernand Braudel's count, the one found, is 236 towns, and the entry now gives his. Cost Disease said New York subway construction runs about $1.5 billion a kilometre. The Transit Costs Project's own New York study puts Phase 1 of the Second Avenue Subway at about $1.7 billion a kilometre, and the entry now says so. In Defense of Bubbles said 85 to 95 per cent of the fibre laid in the 1990s sat dark after the bust. Every account found attributes the range to unnamed analysts, and no study behind it could be opened, so the number is gone.

t: Six superlatives.
b: An audit of claims printed as 'first', 'only' or 'most' found six that said more than a source would. Genghis Khan's entry said he forged the largest contiguous land empire in history; it reached that size under his heirs, after his death in 1227. Rockefeller's called his the largest fortune in American history, with no measure attached; by inflation-adjusted wealth it is not, and by share of the economy it has arguably been overtaken. It now says one of the largest. Edward Thorp's said Beat the Dealer was, by his own description, the first book to prove the house edge could be beaten; his own account of the book does not say so. Why Firms Exist said Coase's paper was largely ignored for thirty years; the paper was cited long before it was put to use, and the entry now quotes only what Coase is on record as saying, that it was little more than an undergraduate essay. Maurice Hilleman's and Fritz Haber's entries stated as the house's own finding what are other people's judgments; both are now worded as such.

t: Five quotations the house had not seen.
b: An audit of quotations checked each one against the document it comes from. Five could not be found in any document the house could open, so they are no longer printed in quotation marks: Confucius on not imposing on others (the translator was never named), Ibn Khaldun on dynasties lasting three generations (not found in the Rosenthal translation the entry relies on), Robert Moses's 'stein' statement (two wordings circulate, and the 1981 obituary that carries it could not be opened), Clair Patterson's 1966 testimony about the Public Health Service, and Thomas Blanton's line about Arkhipov. Each is now given as a paraphrase, which is what the colophon says an unquoted line is. None of them has been shown to be wrong. Separately, Tu Youyou's entry called Rao, Zhang and Li's book the only book-length account in English; Tu's own 2017 book covers the same discovery, as chemistry rather than history.

t: Mark Bertolini's title.
b: The Atlas called Mark Bertolini co-CEO of Oscar Health. He is Oscar's chief executive, with effect from 3 April 2023, when the co-founder Mario Schlosser moved to president of technology (Oscar Health press release, 28 March 2023). The co-CEO post he held before that was at Bridgewater Associates.

t: The Box: the patent, the price and the argument.
b: The Box said Keith Tantlinger persuaded Malcom McLean to give the corner-fitting patent away. The patent (US 3,085,707) was assigned to Sea-Land Service, which released it. No document the house opened says Tantlinger persuaded anyone, and the release is dated both 1963 and 1967, so the entry gives no date. The lede said the cost of loading a ton fell by roughly ninety-seven per cent. The two figures behind it are McLean's accountants' estimate for the Ideal-X, 15.8 cents a ton, against $5.83 for an average break-bulk ship, and the entry now says so. Three claims had no source and are cut: that McLean 'mortgaged everything', that a ship could spend as long in port as at sea, and that ISO work began in 1961 and took roughly a decade. Taiwan's tripling was of its total exports, not its exports to the United States. The disputed section named no one; it now sets Bernhofen, El-Sahli and Kneller (2016) against Hummels (2007).

t: Why Firms Exist: much cited, little used.
b: Why Firms Exist said Coase's 1937 paper was little used for decades before becoming one of the most cited papers in economics. Coase himself described it in 1972 as 'much cited and little used': it was both at once, and the house found no count that ranks it among the most cited. The link to The Box called containerisation 'the largest single reduction in the cost of buying rather than making, ever measured'; Levinson says the freight-cost data of the period will never provide conclusive proof, so nothing was measured, and the line is withdrawn. The disputed section stated a charge — that the theory explains any boundary and predicts nothing — and a reply by Williamson, without naming anyone who made the charge; it now quotes Holmström and Roberts (1998). Coase was 20, not 21, when the 1931 trip began; he had the answer at 21. The figure for his age had been sourced to a University of Chicago page that does not give it.

t: Finding Longitude: the prize was half paid.
b: Finding Longitude said, and correction 3 repeated, that the £20,000 prize was never awarded, to Harrison or to anyone, and that he received £23,065 in all. A special Act of 1765 paid him half the prize, £10,000, once he had explained H4; the other half was never paid, and the £8,750 Parliament voted in 1773 was a grant, not the prize (Jonathan Siegel, 'Law and Longitude', Tulane Law Review, 2009). The £23,065 total had come from Wikipedia, which adds it up two different ways; it is withdrawn, and so is the Wikipedia link in the reading list. The entry also gave H4's Jamaica result, five seconds slow after 81 days, as a measurement. It was Harrison's figure after an allowance for the watch's rate declared once the ship had landed, and the Board called the trial inconclusive; the trial that passed was Barbados in 1764, 39.2 seconds in 47 days. The timeline had Harrison showing H1 to the Royal Society in 1737; what is recorded is the Commissioners' first meeting, on 30 June that year, and their £500. The argument stands: the Board was applying a statute that asked for a method, and that is why it paid half.

t: The colophon: three plates it said were missing.
b: From 22 September the colophon said no image of Ibn Khaldun, Vasily Arkhipov or Emily Warren Roebling had been cleared, while plates of all three were on the shelf, and the pages called two of them portraits. Arkhipov's is a U.S. Navy photograph of submarine B-59 forced to the surface near Cuba on 28–29 October 1962 (National Archives, 428-N-711200): the boat, not the man. Ibn Khaldun's is a page of the Muqaddimah, MS Atıf Efendi 1936, fol. 7a, in the Süleymaniye Library, which Wikimedia Commons records as in his own hand. Roebling's is Carolus-Duran's 1896 portrait in the Brooklyn Museum (1994.69.1), which considers it to have no known copyright restrictions. Each record was opened on 24 October 2026. The two object plates now say what they show, the Roebling credit is printed with the others, and the list of lives with no plate now names Malcom McLean, Rose Blumkin and Henry Singleton, which it had left out.

t: Cleopatra: seven peoples, not nine languages.
b: The life said Cleopatra spoke perhaps nine languages and was reportedly the only Ptolemy in three centuries to learn Egyptian. Plutarch, the source of both (Life of Antony 27), names seven peoples she answered without an interpreter (Ethiopians, Troglodytes, Hebrews, Arabians, Syrians, Medes and Parthians), says she knew the speech of many others, and says the kings of Egypt before her had not even tried to learn the native language. He gives no count of languages and no span of centuries. The entry also said she commanded a navy and managed the wealthiest kingdom in the Mediterranean; neither is in a source the house opened, and both give way to Plutarch's count of what she brought to the war with Octavian: 200 of 800 warships and 20,000 talents. The disputed section said unnamed specialists faulted Stacy Schiff's biography. It named no one, and is withdrawn.

t: Darwin: the delay nobody documented.
b: The life of Charles Darwin opened on the claim that he spent more than twenty years amassing evidence before he dared publish, knowing the storm it would bring, and called him tormented by his theory. That is Adrian Desmond and James Moore's thesis (1991). John van Wyhe, 'Mind the gap', Notes and Records of the Royal Society (2007), shows it has no clear evidence behind it: Darwin's belief in evolution was not a secret, and he was finishing the Beagle books and then the barnacle monograph, which ran to 1854. The entry now says so, and its disputed section, which said there was unusually little to dispute, sets van Wyhe against Desmond and Moore. It also said he spent five years circling the globe; the Beagle sailed on 27 December 1831 and was back at Falmouth on 2 October 1836, four years and nine months. And it said everything from medicine to genetics now rests on his theory, and that he changed humanity's self-understanding more than any thinker since Copernicus; both were the house's opinion with nobody's name on them, and are cut.

t: Einstein: four papers, and the equation that did not reveal the bomb.
b: The life of Albert Einstein said four papers of 1905 remade physics and then described three, folding the fourth, on mass and energy, into the paper on special relativity; they are now listed separately. It said one of them proved the reality of atoms; it proposed a way to count them, and the entry no longer says proved. It said he warned about nuclear weapons whose possibility his own equation had revealed; the chain reaction was Leo Szilard's idea, as this house's life of Szilard records, and the line is withdrawn. Three further claims had no source the house opened and are cut: that he was a committed pacifist, and that GPS and the detection of gravitational waves confirmed his theories. The link to Marie Curie called her the other scientist of 1905; nothing ties her to that year, and the link now rests on the Nobel committees instead. The disputed section was a reading recommendation; it now says what the citation of 1922 left out, and why.

t: Newton: one foot in the Middle Ages is Keynes's line.
b: The life of Isaac Newton ended, and its keep line rested, on the claim that the Scientific Revolution was made by a man with one foot in the medieval world. That is John Maynard Keynes's phrase, from his lecture 'Newton, the Man', read in 1946 after his death: Newton's studies were 'with one foot in the Middle Ages and one foot treading a path for modern science'. The house printed it uncredited, as a finding; it is now Keynes's, with his judgement that the alchemy was 'wholly devoid of scientific value' beside it. The lede said Newton's physics grew partly from a conviction that he was decoding the mind of God; no source the house opened says so, and it is cut. The entry said he invented calculus in parallel with Leibniz. It now says what the record shows instead: the Royal Society's account of the priority dispute, printed anonymously in 1715, was written by Newton.

t: Marie Curie: the notebooks can be read, under protocol.
b: The life of Marie Curie opened on the line that her notebooks are still too radioactive to handle safely. The Bibliothèque nationale de France, which holds them, says the particles absorbed by the paper are still active, and that the volumes may be consulted only on very particular requests under a strict protocol; a reader standing ten minutes before the two shown in its museum receives about 2 nanosieverts, and the BnF says the exhibited notebooks carry no radioactivity beyond the natural kind. The entry said she remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences; the Nobel Foundation's pages the house opened confirm both prizes but do not say only, and the entry no longer does. Five claims had no source the house opened and are cut: that she coined the word radioactivity, that she fainted from hunger over her books, that Polish universities were closed to women, that she drove X-ray units to the front, and that the radiation killed her. The disputed section called Ève Curie's biography hagiographic without naming who says so; it now sets out what the 1903 nomination record shows.

t: Mandela: what he was jailed for, and the offer he refused.
b: The life of Nelson Mandela said he spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years on Robben Island, breaking rocks, and that he was imprisoned for leading the armed wing of the struggle against apartheid. The Nelson Mandela Foundation's prison chronology has him sentenced first, in November 1962, to five years for incitement and leaving the country illegally; convicted of sabotage at Rivonia in June 1964; on Robben Island from 12 June 1964 to 31 March 1982, nearer seventeen years than eighteen; then Pollsmoor and Victor Verster. No source the house opened says how long he broke rocks, and the phrase is cut. Four claims had no source and are cut: that the country was widely expected to collapse into race war, that a single term was a rarity among liberation heroes, what the Truth and Reconciliation Commission chose, and the closing paragraph on forgiveness as statecraft, which was the house's opinion and is now replaced by his own reply of 1985.

t: Lincoln: what the Proclamation freed, and when the letter was written.
b: The life of Abraham Lincoln said he ended American slavery and pushed the Thirteenth Amendment through Congress. The Amendment passed the House on 31 January 1865, 119 to 56, and was ratified on 6 December 1865, after his death; the Emancipation Proclamation, as the National Archives notes, applied only to states in rebellion, exempted parts of them already under Union control, and left the loyal border states untouched. The entry now says so. Five claims had no source the house opened and are cut: the one-room cabin, reading law by firelight, roughly a year of formal schooling, a Gettysburg Address two minutes long, and his assassination days after the Confederacy's surrender. The disputed section said plenty of historians resist David Herbert Donald's thesis without naming one; it now names the argument over the Greeley letter.

t: Borlaug: not doubled, and not as it came.
b: The life of Norman Borlaug said his wheat roughly doubled harvests in India and Pakistan within years and turned looming starvation into self-sufficiency. M. S. Swaminathan, who ran India's programme, gives the rise as 10 million tonnes to 17 million, with no years attached; self-sufficiency in Pakistan by 1970 was Borlaug's forecast in 1964, as the University of Minnesota's Borlaug archive records it. The entry also said he crossbred thousands of varieties; no source the house opened gives a count, and it is cut. The disputed section called Leon Hesser's book an authorized biography and said it does not seriously engage the critics; the house has not read Hesser, and both claims are withdrawn.

t: Matthew Fontaine Maury: nine delegations, and a claim the keep line could not stand behind.
b: The life said representatives of ten maritime nations met at Brussels on 23 August 1853. Maury's own list, in The Physical Geography of the Sea, names France, England, Russia, Sweden and Norway, Holland, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal and the United States: nine delegations, ten countries only if Sweden and Norway are counted apart. Its keep line said the charts shortened the passage to California; that is Maury's claim, which the entry's own disputed section says no table supports, and the line now gives it as his. The entry said he signed the 1851 essay in the Southern Literary Messenger; it is signed with his initials, M. F. M., and now says so. Its account of the end of the Carlotta colony rests on a single New York Tribune dispatch, forwarded by the Mexican republic's minister, and is now credited to it.

t: Richard Arkwright: the trial was over the carding patent.
b: The life's disputed section opened 'Who invented the spinning frame' and said the 1785 trial does not settle it. The patent the Crown cancelled was his second, of 16 December 1775, for machines that prepare cotton for spinning; the frame was patented in 1769 and was not in suit. What Thomas Highs claimed was the use of rollers to draw out cotton, which he dated to 1765 as well as 1767, and John Kay's wife Sarah testified beside her husband, so the Crown's case did not rest on two witnesses. The disputed section now says so. The entry also called Kay a clockmaker on the authority of the 1911 Britannica, which calls him a watchmaker; the trial report, where he calls himself a clock-maker, is now the source.

t: Jamsetji Tata: a quotation one word short, and a page.
b: The source line for Tata's offer to the institute quoted Harris as saying people 'capitalized … and called 30 lacs'. Harris's note on p. 127 reads 'people capitalized it and called it 30 lacs'; the quotation dropped a word without marking it, so it was not verbatim. The same line put the vesting order of 27 May 1909 on p. 152 of Harris; it is on p. 153. Both are now as printed in the 1925 edition, read in the Digital Library of India scan on the Internet Archive.
